finding.claim: POST /profile/avatar fetches an attacker-supplied URL with axios. The only check is that the string starts with https://, so any host, IP, or port is accepted, and redirects are followed without re-validation. An unauthenticated caller can make server-side GET requests to internal hosts, including plain-HTTP internal services and cloud metadata via redirect. The response size is returned, giving a blind size oracle.

trace.note: url = req.body.avatarUrl taken from the JSON body
typeof string and startsWith("https://") only; no URL parse, no host or IP check
axios.get(url) with no maxRedirects=0, no beforeRedirect, no maxContentLength, no timeout, no try/catch; redirects followed by default (axios library default, not verified in repo)
Returns only img.data.length, so the body is not exposed but the size is

finding.guards_checked: server.js:11 scheme prefix check (enforced, return used, but scheme-only: does not constrain host, port, or redirect targets). No private/loopback/link-local/metadata address block. No DNS rebinding protection. No redirect re-validation. No response size cap. Route has no auth middleware.

verdict.guard_found: Only server.js:11, a scheme-only check (typeof string and startsWith("https://")). It does not constrain host, IP, port, or redirect targets. No auth middleware on the route (server.js:9), no hostname allowlist, no private-address block, no maxRedirects=0, and no maxContentLength or timeout at server.js:14.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: req.body.avatarUrl (server.js:10) is unauthenticated input, the only check at server.js:11 is the https:// prefix, and axios.get at server.js:14 follows redirects by default and returns only the body length at server.js:15. Redirect following is axios's Node default, which I know from library behavior rather than from code in this repo. The finding is an SSRF with a blind size oracle, and nothing in the path closes it.

finding.claim: GET /users/:id lets a dot-segment id escape the /v1/users/ path prefix on the fixed upstream host. encodeURIComponent does not encode '.', so id='..' builds a URL that normalizes to /v1/ on users.internal:8080, and the upstream body is returned. Host injection is blocked, so impact is limited to the same upstream host. Rated low. The normalization step is unverified (no node_modules in repo).
finding.source: server.js:18 req.params.id (GET /users/:id, percent-decoded by Express, e.g. /users/%2e%2e yields '..')

trace.note: Route /users/:id, Express decodes the param so %2e%2e becomes '..'
encodeURIComponent leaves '.' unencoded, so id stays '..'
URL becomes http://users.internal:8080/v1/users/.. which normalizes to /v1/ (UNCERTAIN: depends on axios URL normalization)
Upstream response body returned to the client

finding.guards_checked: server.js:7 USER_SVC constant host (SAFE for host injection). server.js:19 encodeURIComponent blocks '/', '?', '#', '@', ':' (SAFE for those). Dot segments '.' and '..' not neutralized (broken control).

verdict.guard_found: none. The only check on this path is server.js:19 encodeURIComponent, which does not encode '.', so dot segments pass through. USER_SVC at server.js:7 is a constant host and closes host injection only.
verdict.reason: server.js:18 reads req.params.id, which Express percent-decodes, so an attacker can send %2e%2e. server.js:19 leaves '..' unchanged, and server.js:20 builds a path that resolves to /v1/ on the fixed host, with the body returned at server.js:21. Impact is limited to one-level path confinement escape on users.internal:8080; the dot-segment normalization in axios is inferred from WHATWG URL behavior, not verified against node_modules.
